recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Hubble photographed the huge galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+223. Its light spent over 5 billion years travelling to reach us. A galaxy cluster is a vast gathering of galaxies held together by gravity, along with large amounts of unseen dark matter.

The cluster's enormous mass bends the light of objects far behind it. This effect, known as gravitational lensing, both magnifies and distorts the background galaxies, stretching and brightening them as seen from Earth.

Lensing can also do something stranger. Because light from a distant object can take more than one path around the cluster, the same object can appear several times in the image. This cluster is producing multiple images of the same distant objects in exactly this way. For astronomers, such repeated images are valuable, because they help map how the cluster's mass is spread out, and they turn the cluster into a natural magnifying glass for studying galaxies that would otherwise be too faint to see.
scale: Light from this cluster took over 5 billion years to reach us, according to the caption.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from the near-infrared end of visible light into the infrared. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Most of this data is infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the faint lensed galaxies need Hubble's exposures to appear.
